corpus.d1:
Retrieval augmentation reduces factual error rates
Grounding a language model in retrieved documents lowers unsupported-claim rates relative to closed-book generation on knowledge-intensive tasks.
corpus.d2:
Cross-encoders outperform bi-encoders for reranking
Jointly encoding query and passage yields higher ranking accuracy than independent encoding, at a cost that scales with the candidate set.
corpus.d3:
Lexical and dense retrieval are complementary
Sparse methods excel on exact term matching while dense methods capture paraphrase; fusing their rankings outperforms either alone.
corpus.d4:
Position bias in long contexts
Models attend more reliably to information at the beginning and end of a long input than to information in the middle.
corpus.d5:
Chunk size affects retrieval precision
Smaller passages improve precision and reduce recall of multi-sentence facts; the optimum is corpus dependent.
corpus.d6:
Multilingual encoders reduce cross-lingual retrieval gaps
Models trained on many languages substantially narrow the recall gap for non-English queries against English corpora.
corpus.d7:
Reciprocal rank fusion is scale invariant
Fusing rankings rather than scores avoids the incomparable-score-scale problem and requires no per-corpus tuning.
corpus.d8:
Optical character recognition error propagates downstream
Transcription error in scanned documents reduces retrieval recall roughly monotonically with character error rate.
corpus.d9:
Quantized vectors trade recall for memory
Scalar and binary quantization reduce index memory by large factors with small measured recall loss when rescoring is applied.
corpus.d10:
Judge models introduce evaluation variance
Unpinned evaluator models and non-zero temperature produce metric variation comparable to real quality differences.
